benchmark.title: Agent onboarding benchmark
benchmark.method: Two isolated autonomous agents, each starting from the same prerequisite state: a populated .env with a valid kh_ organisation key, on Base Sepolia, with no prior KeeperHub knowledge in context. The baseline arm was given only public KeeperHub documentation and was explicitly forbidden from reading this repository. The treatment arm was given only the repository's README. Both were required to reach the same finish line: a transaction where KeeperHub's execution record, a public Base Sepolia receipt, and a decoded event all agree, verified by the agent itself rather than taken from tool output.
benchmark.notHumanStudy: Agents, not humans. This is an agent onboarding benchmark and is never described as a human UX study. Agents read faster than people and do not get frustrated, so the absolute times are not human times. The comparison between arms is the measurement; the absolute numbers are not.

arms.name: Baseline
arms.operation: WETH9.approve, chosen by the agent as a zero-value write

arms.name: Recovery
arms.given: a real post-submit response loss, injected
arms.note: Two broadcast requests reached KeeperHub. One transaction exists onchain, counted by eth_getLogs on the run's unique challenge topic.

benchmark.caveat: Read this before the numbers. (1) The arms did not solve the same problem. The baseline agent had to choose a contract, invent a verification method for it, and hand-write keccak to decode an Approval topic. The treatment arm called a canary purpose-built to be trivially verifiable, emitting an indexed challenge the tool generated, with topic0 pinned in config and the decoder shipped. This benchmark substantially measures a purpose-built tool beating general documentation at the exact task it was built for. (2) The docsOpened figures are not like-for-like: the baseline count includes URLs the agent guessed and got 404s from, while the treatment count is one file that was handed to it, requiring no discovery. (3) n=1 per arm, timings self-captured by the agents, and the treatment log was written by the same agent asked to review the product. An earlier version of this field claimed the comparison understates rather than overstates the difference; that direction was asserted rather than measured, and given (1) it may well be backwards. An external audit flagged all three points.
notMeasured: human onboarding time, in either arm

priorRun.note: An earlier treatment run was executed before README.md existed, so the agent had only --help to work from. It reached a first transaction in 58s and full independent verification in 2m 16s across 3 commands. It is not counted in the comparison above because its starting condition differed from the baseline arm's, but it is recorded here because it is a harder condition than a real user faces and it found three real defects, all since fixed.
defectsFound: the proof capsule was written over the run record, so status reported a successful run as never having happened
--resume on a completed run crashed with an unhandled error
--json on a preflight emitted only two fields

defectsFoundByTreatmentArm.note: The treatment agent was asked to review as well as measure. It found six further defects, all outside the proof path, and all fixed before publication.
items: README claimed the manifest summarised every verified run, but the manifest needed a separate command; the CLI now regenerates it after a verified run
CLAIMS.md froze a failure-code count that the generated docs had already moved past; the claim now cites the generated artifact instead of a number
unknown flags such as --exec ran a silent preflight and exited 0; unknown flags and arguments are now rejected with exit 64
--resume with no run id silently degraded to a preflight; it now errors and points at status
a run record predating the capsule fix reported a stale stage; the final stage is now persisted
npm's banner broke piping --json into jq; the README now shows npm run --silent

tests.note: Unit and state-machine tests, runnable from a fresh clone with no npm install. The live fault-injection acceptance test is separate, needs credentials, and is run with npm run test:acceptance; its result is in evidence/recovery/.
